case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the IDEA's administrative exhaustion requirement bars a deaf student from bringing an ADA claim in federal court after settling his IDEA claim, when the ADA seeks relief unavailable under the IDEA.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Individuals with Disabilities Education Act (IDEA), 20 U.S.C. § 1415(l); Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA), 42 U.S.C. § 12101 et seq.; also implicating the Persons with Disabilities Civil Rights Act (PWDCRA) under Michigan state law.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Miguel Luna Perez argues that because he already settled his IDEA claim through administrative proceedings, and because his ADA claims seek compensatory damages — a form of relief entirely unavailable under the IDEA — he should not be required to exhaust IDEA administrative remedies before pursuing his ADA lawsuit. He further contends that the 'gravamen' test established in Fry v. Napoleon Community Schools should not mandate exhaustion where the relief sought is categorically different from what IDEA provides, and that standard futility and inadequacy exceptions to exhaustion should apply.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Sturgis Public Schools and its Board of Education argue that the IDEA's exhaustion requirement under § 1415(l) applies to Perez's ADA claims because the core grievance — the alleged denial of a free appropriate public education (FAPE) — is fundamentally an IDEA-type claim regardless of how it is pleaded or what label is attached to it. Respondents contend that allowing plaintiffs to bypass IDEA exhaustion simply by framing claims under the ADA or settling the IDEA portion would undermine the administrative framework Congress established for resolving special education disputes.
key_precedents: Fry v. Napoleon Community Schools, 137 S. Ct. 743 (2017) — established the 'gravamen' test for determining when IDEA exhaustion is required for non-IDEA claims
Honig v. Doe, 484 U.S. 305 (1988) — recognized futility and inadequacy exceptions to IDEA exhaustion requirement
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007) — standard for Rule 12(b)(6) motions to dismiss
Center for Bio-Ethical Reform, Inc. v. Napolitano, 648 F.3d 365 (6th Cir. 2011) — Sixth Circuit standard requiring courts to accept factual allegations as true on motions to dismiss
Education of the Handicapped Act (1970) — predecessor statute to the IDEA, relevant to legislative history and congressional intent

John Roberts.reasoning: The conference is in remarkable agreement, and I find the core textual argument — that § 1415(l)'s exhaustion requirement is simply not triggered when the relief sought is categorically unavailable under the IDEA — to be sound and minimally sufficient to resolve this case. Justice Kagan's careful attention to Congress's parallel usage of 'relief' in § 1415(i)(3)(D)(i)(III) strengthens the textual case by showing Congress understood 'relief' to mean specific remedy, not general subject matter. Justice Jackson's point about the perverse incentive structure — that requiring exhaustion after settlement would discourage schools from settling IDEA claims, thereby undermining both statutes — reinforces that the Sixth Circuit's rule produces consequences Congress could not have intended when it enacted § 1415(l) specifically to preserve independent anti-discrimination remedies after Smith v. Robinson. As Chief Justice, I would assign the opinion with instructions to rest the holding on the narrowest ground: the plain text of § 1415(l) does not require exhaustion when the relief sought — compensatory damages — is categorically unavailable under the IDEA, with Perez's prior settlement serving as an independent and sufficient alternative basis, thereby avoiding any broader pronouncements about the scope of the futility doctrine.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: My colleagues have collectively reinforced what the text of § 1415(l) plainly commands: exhaustion is required only when a plaintiff seeks 'relief that is also available under' the IDEA, and compensatory damages are categorically unavailable under the IDEA's administrative scheme. Justice Kagan's careful attention to Congress's own parallel usage of 'relief' in § 1415(i)(3)(D)(i)(III) — comparing 'relief finally obtained' to settlement offers — further confirms that 'relief' means remedy in the specific, legally operative sense, not merely any form of redress touching on educational grievances. Justice Jackson's point about the perverse incentive structure created by the Sixth Circuit's rule is particularly compelling from a structural standpoint: requiring students to reject IDEA settlements to preserve ADA damages claims would undermine both statutes simultaneously, a result Congress manifestly did not intend when it enacted § 1415(l) specifically to preserve independent anti-discrimination enforcement after Smith v. Robinson. The strongest argument for respondent — that allowing plaintiffs to circumvent exhaustion by appending a damages claim would swallow the exhaustion requirement — fails because the IDEA's administrative process genuinely cannot award compensatory damages under any circumstances, meaning no artful pleading is occurring; the relief sought is structurally distinct, not merely repackaged.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: I find myself in substantial agreement with Justice Roberts and Justice Thomas that the plain text of § 1415(l) is dispositive here — the exhaustion requirement is triggered only when a plaintiff seeks 'relief that is also available under' the IDEA, and compensatory damages are simply not available under the IDEA's administrative scheme by any reading of the statute. Justice Kagan's point about Congress's parallel usage of 'relief' in § 1415(i)(3)(D)(i)(III) — comparing 'relief finally obtained' to settlement offers — reinforces that 'relief' means remedy in the concrete sense, not merely the underlying grievance, which strengthens the textual case considerably. The strongest argument for the respondent would be that the Sixth Circuit's approach prevents artful pleading around IDEA exhaustion, but as Justice Barrett correctly notes, Fry's gravamen test already addresses that concern, and where the remedy sought is categorically outside the IDEA's remedial scheme, no amount of artful pleading analysis changes the statutory text. The fact that Perez already completed IDEA administrative proceedings through settlement further satisfies any residual exhaustion concern, making the Sixth Circuit's rule not merely textually unsupported but practically perverse.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: I am in full agreement with Justice Jackson's textual analysis that § 1415(l)'s plain language is dispositive — exhaustion is conditioned on seeking 'relief that is also available under the IDEA,' and compensatory damages are simply not available through IDEA administrative proceedings, full stop. Justice Jackson's additional point about the perverse incentive structure created by the Sixth Circuit's rule particularly resonates with me: requiring students to reject IDEA settlements to preserve ADA damages claims would punish good-faith participation in administrative proceedings and incentivize schools to withhold settlements strategically, harming the very vulnerable disabled students both statutes are designed to protect. Chief Justice Roberts correctly identifies that Perez already completed administrative proceedings through settlement, meaning the core purposes of exhaustion — developing a factual record and allowing agency expertise to operate — have been substantially served, making further exhaustion not just futile but actively counterproductive. The strongest argument for respondent would be that the 'gravamen' test from Fry requires exhaustion whenever the underlying grievance concerns FAPE regardless of the remedy sought, but this reading cannot be squared with the statute's text, which focuses specifically on the relief sought, not the nature of the underlying claim — and Fry itself explicitly reserved this precise question, meaning it cannot be read to resolve it against Perez.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: I find myself in strong agreement with my colleagues across the ideological spectrum, and Justice Jackson's point about the perverse incentive structure deserves particular emphasis: a rule requiring exhaustion before settlement would force disabled students to reject full IDEA settlements to preserve ADA damages claims, which would undermine both statutes simultaneously and cannot reflect congressional intent. The textual argument is straightforward — § 1415(l)'s plain language conditions exhaustion on seeking 'relief that is also available under' the IDEA, and compensatory damages are simply not available under the IDEA by any reading. Justice Roberts correctly identifies this as a minimalist, statute-respecting resolution that honors Congress's deliberate choice in enacting § 1415(l) to preserve independent anti-discrimination remedies after Smith v. Robinson. The strongest counterargument — that the 'gravamen' test from Fry should focus on the underlying grievance rather than the specific remedy — fails because Fry itself reserved this precise question and because reading 'relief' to mean 'grievance' would render the word 'also available under' essentially meaningless, violating basic canons of statutory construction.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: My colleagues have collectively and persuasively reinforced what the plain text of § 1415(l) compels: exhaustion is required only when a plaintiff seeks 'relief that is also available under' the IDEA, and compensatory damages are simply not available under the IDEA by any reading of that word. Justice Kagan's observation that Congress itself used 'relief' to mean 'remedy' in § 1415(i)(3)(D)(i)(III) — comparing 'relief finally obtained' to settlement offers — is particularly useful textualist evidence that 'relief' in § 1415(l) refers to the specific remedy sought, not the general subject matter of the dispute. The strongest argument for the respondent would be that allowing plaintiffs to circumvent exhaustion simply by appending a damages claim risks strategic pleading that undermines the IDEA's administrative scheme — but Fry's gravamen test already addresses that concern by looking past artful pleading to the true nature of the claim, and where compensatory damages are the genuine and sole remedy sought, no amount of gravamen analysis can conjure IDEA availability where none exists. Justice Jackson's point that requiring exhaustion after settlement would perversely incentivize schools to withhold settlements further confirms that the Sixth Circuit's rule produces consequences Congress could not have intended when it enacted § 1415(l) specifically to preserve independent anti-discrimination remedies.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: I find myself in substantial agreement with Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan that the plain text of § 1415(l) is dispositive here — the exhaustion requirement is conditioned on the plaintiff 'seeking relief that is also available under' the IDEA, and compensatory damages are simply not available under the IDEA by any reading of the statute. Justice Kagan's point about Congress's parallel usage of 'relief' in § 1415(i)(3)(D)(i)(III) as referring to remedy rather than the underlying grievance is particularly persuasive from a textualist standpoint and reinforces that 'relief' means the specific remedy sought, not the general subject matter of the complaint. The strongest counterargument the respondents could raise — that allowing plaintiffs to circumvent exhaustion by characterizing their claims as damages-only would undermine the IDEA's administrative framework — is addressed by Fry's gravamen test, which already guards against artful pleading, and in any event Perez actually completed IDEA proceedings through settlement, meaning the administrative purposes of exhaustion have been substantially served. As an institutionalist, I also note that requiring exhaustion of a process structurally incapable of providing the requested remedy would damage the Court's credibility in faithfully applying statutory text and would effectively nullify Congress's deliberate choice in § 1415(l) to preserve independent anti-discrimination remedies after Smith v. Robinson.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: I find myself in substantial agreement with my colleagues across the ideological spectrum, which itself reflects the strength of the textual argument. Justice Thomas correctly identifies that the plain text of § 1415(l) is the beginning and end of the analysis: exhaustion is conditioned on seeking 'relief that is also available under' the IDEA, and compensatory damages are simply not available under the IDEA's administrative scheme — a point respondents cannot seriously contest. Justice Kagan's observation that Congress's own parallel usage of 'relief' in § 1415(i)(3)(D)(i)(III) confirms that the term means remedy, not merely the underlying grievance, further reinforces the textual case. The strongest counterargument would be that courts should look to the gravamen of the complaint rather than the label of the remedy to prevent artful pleading, but Fry itself was designed to address that concern in the context of equitable relief that IDEA could provide — it cannot be stretched to require exhaustion of a process structurally incapable of awarding the remedy sought, and Perez's prior settlement further forecloses any argument that exhaustion purposes remain unserved.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: I remain firmly with the Petitioner, and I find the convergence of my colleagues' reasoning — from Justice Thomas's textualism to Justice Sotomayor's practical justice analysis — powerfully reinforces what the statute plainly says: exhaustion is required only when the plaintiff seeks 'relief that is also available under' the IDEA, and compensatory damages are simply not available under the IDEA by anyone's account. The strongest argument for the Respondent would be that the 'gravamen' test from Fry should look past the remedy label to the underlying educational grievance, but as Justice Kagan correctly notes, Congress used 'relief' in § 1415(l) in its ordinary legal sense as remedy — not as a synonym for the underlying factual dispute — and that textual choice is dispositive. My background as a public defender makes me acutely sensitive to how procedural exhaustion requirements can function as de facto barriers that extinguish substantive rights, and requiring Miguel Perez to exhaust an administrative process that has already concluded through settlement and that could never award the damages he seeks would transform a prudential gatekeeping mechanism into an instrument of injustice that Congress never intended when it enacted § 1415(l) specifically to preserve independent civil rights enforcement after Smith v. Robinson. The unanimity of my colleagues across very different judicial methodologies — textualist, pragmatist, and everything in between — confirms that this is not a close case.

John Roberts.reasoning: The plain text of § 1415(l) conditions the exhaustion requirement on the plaintiff 'seeking relief that is also available under' the IDEA, and compensatory damages are categorically unavailable under the IDEA — making the exhaustion requirement logically inapplicable on its face. Furthermore, Perez already completed administrative proceedings through settlement, meaning the core purposes of exhaustion — developing a factual record and allowing the agency to apply its expertise — have been served, rendering further exhaustion both futile and unnecessary under Honig v. Doe. Fry v. Napoleon Community Schools explicitly reserved the question of whether exhaustion is required when the relief sought is unavailable under the IDEA, and the narrow, textually grounded resolution here — that § 1415(l)'s plain language simply does not reach claims for relief the IDEA cannot provide — is precisely the kind of minimalist, statute-respecting ruling that avoids unnecessary constitutional tension while honoring Congress's deliberate choice in enacting § 1415(l) to preserve distinct anti-discrimination remedies after Smith v. Robinson. Requiring exhaustion of a completed administrative process to obtain relief that process could never award would elevate procedural formalism over congressional intent and institutional coherence.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The plain text of § 1415(l) conditions exhaustion only when a plaintiff seeks 'relief that is also available under' the IDEA, and compensatory damages are categorically unavailable under the IDEA's administrative scheme — a point the respondents themselves do not seriously contest. As a textualist and originalist, I must give effect to the words Congress actually enacted, not an expansive reading that would swallow non-IDEA statutory remedies whole; the legislative history further confirms Congress deliberately rejected a broader exhaustion mandate that would have applied wherever any IDEA remedy existed. Fry v. Napoleon Community Schools reinforced that the exhaustion inquiry turns on the nature of the relief sought, and where the relief sought — money damages — cannot be obtained through IDEA administrative proceedings under any circumstances, requiring exhaustion would be a futile exercise that the statute's own text does not compel. Moreover, Perez already participated in and settled IDEA administrative proceedings, meaning the administrative record has been developed and the purposes of exhaustion — allowing agencies to apply expertise and correct their own errors — have been substantially served, further undermining any textual or structural basis for barring his ADA claim.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Under a textualist reading of § 1415(l), the exhaustion requirement applies only when a plaintiff seeks 'relief that is also available under' the IDEA — and compensatory damages are categorically unavailable under the IDEA, making exhaustion both textually inapplicable and practically futile. Fry v. Napoleon Community Schools established that courts must look to the gravamen of the complaint, but critically, the plaintiff is 'master of his claim,' and where the relief sought — monetary damages — cannot be obtained through IDEA administrative proceedings, requiring exhaustion serves no congressional purpose and produces the perverse result of forcing a plaintiff through a process incapable of providing the remedy he seeks. Furthermore, Perez already completed IDEA administrative proceedings through settlement, meaning any exhaustion concern has been practically satisfied, and the futility exception recognized in Honig v. Doe independently bars dismissal. Allowing the Sixth Circuit's overbroad reading of § 1415(l) to stand would effectively nullify Congress's express intent in enacting that provision — to preserve the ADA and Rehabilitation Act as independent enforcement vehicles separate from the IDEA framework.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The text of IDEA § 1415(l) requires exhaustion only when a plaintiff is 'seeking relief that is also available under the IDEA,' and compensatory damages are categorically unavailable through IDEA administrative proceedings, making exhaustion both textually inapplicable and functionally futile. As Fry v. Napoleon Community Schools explicitly left open the question of whether exhaustion is required when the specific remedy sought cannot be awarded by an IDEA hearing officer, the answer must be no — requiring Miguel Perez to exhaust an administrative process that cannot provide his requested relief serves no meaningful purpose and imposes a purely procedural barrier that Congress never intended. The practical impact on vulnerable disabled students like Miguel — who was systematically denied an interpreter and a meaningful education for years — is severe: forcing exhaustion here would effectively nullify ADA damages claims for students who have already engaged the IDEA process, creating an unjust and irrational result that punishes good-faith participation in administrative proceedings. Honig v. Doe's recognition of futility and inadequacy exceptions, reinforced by Smith v. Berryhill's reaffirmation that exhaustion is unnecessary when it 'would serve no meaningful purpose,' compels the conclusion that Perez's ADA claim may proceed directly in federal court.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Under Fry v. Napoleon Community Schools, the 'gravamen' test asks whether the plaintiff is the 'master of the claim' and whether the complaint actually seeks relief available under the IDEA — and compensatory damages are categorically unavailable under the IDEA, meaning exhaustion of IDEA administrative remedies cannot provide the relief Perez seeks. Furthermore, Perez already completed IDEA administrative proceedings through settlement, satisfying any exhaustion purpose of developing a factual record and allowing the agency to apply its expertise, making further exhaustion both futile and inadequate under Honig v. Doe. A workable, textually coherent reading of § 1415(l) cannot require a plaintiff to exhaust a process that is structurally incapable of providing the remedy he seeks, as that would transform exhaustion from a prudential gatekeeping mechanism into an insurmountable barrier to vindicating independent statutory rights under the ADA.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The text of § 1415(l) is dispositive: it requires exhaustion only when a plaintiff 'seeks relief that is also available under the IDEA,' and compensatory damages are categorically unavailable under the IDEA, making the exhaustion requirement inapplicable on its face to Perez's ADA claim. Napoleon Community Schools was designed to prevent plaintiffs from artfully pleading around IDEA exhaustion to obtain the same equitable relief IDEA provides, not to erect procedural barriers when the plaintiff seeks fundamentally different remedies that the IDEA's administrative process is structurally incapable of providing. Doe — exhaustion serves no purpose when the administrative process has concluded and cannot furnish the remedy sought, and forcing disabled students to reject full IDEA settlements to preserve distinct civil rights claims would perversely incentivize schools to withhold settlements, undermining both statutes. As a former public defender acutely aware of how procedural barriers disproportionately burden vulnerable populations, I find that the Sixth Circuit's rule would effectively extinguish legitimate civil rights claims for disabled students through procedural formalism Congress never intended.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the IDEA requires a plaintiff to exhaust its administrative procedures before bringing a disability discrimination claim under the ADA when the underlying IDEA claim has already been resolved through settlement.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Individuals with Disabilities Education Act (IDEA), 20 U.S.C. § 1400 et seq., specifically the exhaustion requirement under § 1415(l), in conjunction with the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA), 42 U.S.C. § 12101 et seq., and the Persons with Disabilities Civil Rights Act (PWDCRA)
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Miguel Luna Perez argues that because his IDEA claim was already resolved through settlement, the IDEA exhaustion requirement should not apply as a bar to his ADA claims. He contends that requiring exhaustion under these circumstances would be futile and inadequate, as the administrative process has already run its course through settlement. He further argues that the gravamen of his ADA complaint seeks relief not available under IDEA, making exhaustion unnecessary under the standard established in Fry v. Napoleon Community Schools.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Sturgis Public Schools and its Board of Education argue that Perez's ADA and PWDCRA claims seek the same type of relief available under IDEA, meaning the IDEA exhaustion requirement still applies regardless of the prior settlement. Respondents contend that the core or 'gravamen' of Perez's complaint is fundamentally rooted in the denial of a free appropriate public education (FAPE), which falls squarely within IDEA's administrative framework, and that artful pleading cannot circumvent the exhaustion mandate.
key_precedents: Fry v. Napoleon Community Schools, 137 S. Ct. 743 (2017) - established the 'gravamen' test for determining when IDEA exhaustion is required for non-IDEA claims
Honig v. Doe, 484 U.S. 305 (1988) - addressed IDEA exhaustion exceptions including futility, both legal and practical
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007) - established pleading standards for Rule 12(b)(6) motions to dismiss
Center for Bio-Ethical Reform, Inc. v. Napolitano, 648 F.3d 365 (6th Cir. 2011) - Sixth Circuit standard for accepting factual allegations on motion to dismiss
Education of the Handicapped Act (1970) - predecessor statute to IDEA, relevant to legislative history

John Roberts.reasoning: The conference has reached a remarkable degree of consensus, and I find myself in agreement with the core reasoning articulated by Justice Kagan, whose Fry framework provides the most workable and institutionally sound basis for decision. The narrow ground I would emphasize — consistent with my minimalist approach — is that § 1415(l)'s exhaustion requirement is simply not triggered when the relief sought (compensatory damages) is categorically unavailable under IDEA, and separately, that requiring exhaustion through an administrative process already concluded by settlement would be textually unsupported and practically futile under Honig. I would resist the broader holdings some colleagues suggest and instead write narrowly: we need not resolve every edge case of the Fry gravamen test, but only hold that where (1) the plaintiff seeks relief IDEA cannot provide, and (2) the administrative process has already run its course through settlement, § 1415(l) poses no bar. As Chief Justice, I would assign the majority opinion with an eye toward a narrow, durable holding that commands the broadest consensus and leaves the most difficult hypotheticals for another day.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: My colleagues have collectively reinforced the textual and structural case for the petitioner, and I find the convergence of originalist and textualist reasoning compelling. Justice Gorsuch correctly identifies that § 1415(l)'s plain text requires exhaustion 'before the filing of a civil action' seeking relief 'also available under' IDEA — a condition that is simply not met when (1) the administrative process has already concluded through settlement and (2) the relief sought is compensatory damages unavailable under IDEA's remedial scheme. The strongest argument for the respondent would be that Congress intended § 1415(l) to function as a broad channeling mechanism ensuring educational disputes flow through IDEA's expert administrative process regardless of how they are labeled, but this argument founders on the legislative history Justice Gorsuch highlights: Congress explicitly rejected the NSBA's broader exhaustion proposal, confirming that § 1415(l) was narrowly crafted to cover only unresolved claims seeking IDEA-available relief. Requiring exhaustion of a completed, settled administrative process would not merely be futile under Honig — it would be a textual nullity, demanding compliance with a statutory condition that by its own terms no longer applies.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Kagan's articulation of the Fry gravamen test, which she authored, reinforces my textualist reading of § 1415(l): the statute's plain text conditions exhaustion on seeking 'relief that is also available under' IDEA, and compensatory damages are simply not available in IDEA administrative proceedings, full stop. Justice Gorsuch correctly notes that the statute requires exhaustion 'before filing,' not re-exhaustion of a process already completed through settlement — demanding Perez restart administrative proceedings that have concluded would have no textual anchor in the statute whatsoever. The strongest argument for the Respondent would be that the settlement did not constitute genuine exhaustion and that Perez strategically settled to circumvent the exhaustion requirement, but even accepting that concern, the text of § 1415(l) does not condition exhaustion on the nature of how prior proceedings concluded — it conditions exhaustion on whether the relief sought is available under IDEA, and money damages are not. The unanimity of my colleagues across ideological lines on this point, while not determinative, reflects that the textual and doctrinal case for Petitioner is genuinely strong and not merely a product of policy preferences.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: I am fully aligned with Justice Kagan's articulation of the Fry gravamen test and her observation that requiring exhaustion through a process already concluded by settlement would be 'structurally incoherent' — this captures precisely the practical absurdity that my judicial philosophy demands we avoid when vulnerable populations like disabled students are at stake. The strongest argument for Respondent would be that § 1415(l)'s exhaustion requirement serves a channeling function ensuring administrative expertise is brought to bear before courts intervene, but as Justice Gorsuch correctly notes from a textualist perspective, the statute's plain text conditions exhaustion on seeking 'relief also available under' IDEA, and compensatory damages simply are not available there. The settlement of Perez's IDEA claim is not a loophole but rather confirmation that the administrative process has served its purpose — channeling the FAPE dispute through the appropriate forum — and the ADA's independent remedial scheme for discrimination-based monetary relief was deliberately preserved by Congress in the 1986 HCPA. Forcing Perez to re-exhaust would impose a hollow procedural burden that serves none of exhaustion's rationales while effectively nullifying Congress's deliberate choice to maintain the ADA as a robust, independent vehicle for disabled students' civil rights.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: I remain firmly in the Petitioner camp, and I'm gratified that my colleagues across the ideological spectrum have converged on a reading that tracks the gravamen framework I articulated in Fry. Justice Thomas raises the most textually precise formulation — that § 1415(l)'s exhaustion requirement 'presupposes an incomplete and available administrative process' — which reinforces my own view that the provision simply has no operative purchase once the IDEA proceedings have concluded through settlement. The strongest argument for Respondent would be that settlement doesn't constitute genuine exhaustion and that Congress intended § 1415(l) to channel all disability-related educational claims through administrative review regardless of how prior proceedings concluded; but this argument founders on the statutory text itself, which conditions exhaustion on seeking 'relief also available under' IDEA — and compensatory damages are categorically unavailable there. Justice Sotomayor correctly identifies that treating the settlement as a perpetual bar would effectively resurrect the pre-§ 1415(l) regime Congress deliberately rejected, and the workability principle that animates my pragmatic textualism cannot countenance a reading that transforms a procedural gateway into an absolute jurisdictional barrier serving no cognizable statutory purpose.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: My colleagues across the ideological spectrum have converged on the correct textual reading of § 1415(l), and I find no argument from the respondent's side that genuinely undermines my analysis. Justice Kagan's articulation of the gravamen test from Fry — which she authored — confirms that the exhaustion requirement is not triggered when the relief sought is unavailable under IDEA, and compensatory damages are categorically outside IDEA's remedial framework. Justice Thomas correctly identifies the originalist point that Congress deliberately rejected broader exhaustion proposals, which forecloses any argument that § 1415(l) was meant to sweep in claims seeking relief IDEA cannot provide. The strongest argument for the respondent would be that settlement of an IDEA claim does not constitute completion of the administrative process, but this fails on the text: § 1415(l) requires exhaustion 'before filing,' and a concluded settlement means the administrative process has run its course — demanding re-exhaustion of a completed process has no textual anchor in the statute and would produce the absurd result of requiring exhaustion of a process that no longer exists.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: I find myself in strong agreement with Justice Kagan's articulation of the gravamen test from Fry, which she authored, and Justice Roberts' institutionally grounded reading of § 1415(l) — both converge on the conclusion that exhaustion cannot be required when the administrative process has already concluded through settlement and the relief sought (compensatory damages) is categorically unavailable under IDEA. The strongest argument for the Respondent would be that § 1415(l)'s exhaustion requirement is a categorical rule that must be satisfied regardless of the form of relief sought, to prevent plaintiffs from artfully pleading around IDEA's administrative framework — but this argument fails because the statutory text itself conditions exhaustion on whether relief is 'also available under' IDEA, and money damages simply are not. Justice Gorsuch's textualist point is particularly compelling: the statute requires exhaustion 'before filing,' not re-exhaustion of a process already completed, and reading the provision otherwise would transform a procedural gateway into an absurd perpetual bar. From an institutionalist standpoint, a ruling for Petitioner here preserves the complementary statutory architecture Congress deliberately designed when it enacted both IDEA and the ADA as independent remedial vehicles, which is the kind of structural coherence the Court should protect.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: My colleagues have collectively reinforced what I view as the most textually sound reading of § 1415(l): the exhaustion requirement is triggered only when a plaintiff seeks 'relief that is also available under' IDEA, and compensatory damages are categorically unavailable under IDEA's administrative framework. Justice Kagan's articulation of the Fry gravamen test — which she authored — is particularly persuasive in confirming that the inquiry focuses on the substance of what relief is sought, not merely whether the underlying facts could theoretically have been channeled through IDEA proceedings. Justice Thomas adds an important originalist dimension: the legislative history of the 1986 HCPA amendment shows Congress deliberately rejected broader exhaustion proposals, confirming that § 1415(l) was not designed to sweep in claims seeking remedies outside IDEA's scope. The strongest counterargument from the Respondent's position would be that allowing settlement to satisfy exhaustion creates a loophole permitting plaintiffs to manufacture exhaustion through minimal IDEA filings before pursuing ADA damages claims — but this concern is addressed by Fry's gravamen test itself, which independently asks whether the ADA claim's substance is really about FAPE denial, not merely whether some IDEA proceeding occurred.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: I find myself in strong agreement with Justice Kagan's articulation of the gravamen test from Fry, which she authored, and her observation that requiring exhaustion through a process that has already concluded would be 'structurally incoherent' — this resonates deeply with my concern for procedural fairness and meaningful access to justice. The strongest argument for the Respondent would be that § 1415(l)'s exhaustion requirement serves an expertise-channeling function that should apply regardless of settlement, but this argument fails because: first, the settlement has already allowed the administrative body to exercise whatever expertise it possesses regarding the educational context; and second, compensatory damages under the ADA address discrimination harms that IDEA hearing officers have no expertise to evaluate whatsoever. Justice Sotomayor correctly identifies that treating Perez as 'master of his own claim' under Fry means we look to what relief his ADA complaint actually seeks — monetary compensation for disability discrimination — not what relief he could theoretically have sought. From my perspective as a former public defender who has seen how procedural barriers can effectively nullify substantive rights, I am particularly attentive to the reality that requiring re-exhaustion here would not serve any of the rationales underlying the exhaustion doctrine but would instead function as a practical denial of civil rights remedies to a disabled student.

John Roberts.reasoning: The narrow question here is whether IDEA's exhaustion requirement under § 1415(l) bars Perez's ADA claims when the administrative process has already run its course through settlement of his IDEA claim. Requiring exhaustion under these circumstances would be both futile and inadequate — the very exceptions recognized in Honig v. Doe, 484 U.S. 305 (1988) — because there is no longer any administrative forum capable of providing relief, as the IDEA proceeding was dismissed following settlement. Furthermore, applying Fry's gravamen test, to the extent Perez's ADA claims seek compensatory damages for past harms — relief categorically unavailable under IDEA — the exhaustion requirement of § 1415(l) is simply not triggered, because the 'relief sought' is not 'also available' under IDEA. The institutionally minimalist and textually faithful reading of § 1415(l) counsels against extending the exhaustion bar to circumstances where the administrative process has been fully and finally concluded, as doing so would transform exhaustion from a procedural gateway into an absolute jurisdictional bar untethered from the statute's purpose.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The plain text of § 1415(l) requires exhaustion 'before the filing of a civil action' seeking 'relief that is also available under' IDEA — a textual command that presupposes an incomplete and available administrative process. When a plaintiff has already resolved his IDEA claims through settlement, the administrative procedures have run their course, and there is no remaining process to exhaust; demanding further exhaustion would be a nullity with no textual basis in the statute. As an originalist matter, the 1986 HCPA amendment's exhaustion provision was narrowly crafted — Congress explicitly rejected broader exhaustion proposals — indicating the provision was meant to channel unresolved IDEA-type claims through administrative processes, not to create a perpetual barrier after those processes have concluded. Furthermore, to the extent Perez's ADA claims seek compensatory damages not available under IDEA, the gravamen test from Fry v. Napoleon Community Schools confirms exhaustion is not required for relief the IDEA cannot provide, and forcing exhaustion of a fully settled matter would be textually unsupported and practically futile under Honig v. Doe.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The plain text of § 1415(l) conditions the exhaustion requirement on whether the plaintiff seeks 'relief' that is 'available' under IDEA. Here, Miguel Perez seeks money damages through his ADA claim, which all parties concede is not available under IDEA's administrative framework. A textualist reading of § 1415(l) therefore compels the conclusion that exhaustion is not required when the specific remedy sought — compensatory damages — lies entirely outside IDEA's administrative remedial scheme, as established by the gravamen analysis in Fry v. Napoleon Community Schools. Furthermore, requiring additional exhaustion after a completed settlement would be a futile exercise inconsistent with the statutory text and the well-established futility exception recognized in Honig v. Doe, as the administrative process has already run its course and cannot provide the damages relief Perez now seeks.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Under Fry v. Napoleon Community Schools, the exhaustion requirement of § 1415(l) applies only when the 'gravamen' of the complaint seeks relief available under IDEA — here, Perez's ADA claims seek compensatory damages for discrimination that IDEA's administrative process cannot provide, meaning exhaustion would be both futile and inadequate. The settlement of the underlying IDEA claim has already run the administrative process to its conclusion, and requiring Perez to re-exhaust those same procedures would be a hollow formality that serves none of the purposes exhaustion is designed to achieve, as recognized in Honig v. Doe's futility exception. Treating Perez as 'master of his own claim,' as Fry explicitly commands, his ADA complaint's essential character targets disability-based discrimination and seeks monetary relief unavailable through IDEA's administrative framework — the Sixth Circuit majority's approach effectively resurrects the pre-§ 1415(l) regime that Congress specifically rejected when it enacted that provision to preserve ADA and Section 504 as independent remedial vehicles. Requiring exhaustion under these circumstances would impose a severe practical burden on vulnerable disabled students and their families, undermining Congress's deliberate choice to maintain separate, robust antidiscrimination protections alongside IDEA.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Under the gravamen test I articulated in Fry v. Napoleon Community Schools, the exhaustion requirement of IDEA § 1415(l) applies only when the substance of a complaint seeks relief 'available' under IDEA — but where an IDEA claim has already been resolved through settlement, requiring exhaustion of the same administrative process would be both futile and structurally incoherent, as there is no longer any administrative remedy to exhaust. More critically, Perez's ADA claims seek compensatory damages for harms extending beyond the denial of a FAPE — relief that IDEA's administrative framework cannot provide — meaning the gravamen of his complaint reaches beyond what IDEA covers, satisfying the Fry exception. The two diagnostic hypotheticals from Fry cut in both directions here, but the workability principle that animates § 1415(l) cannot plausibly demand exhaustion through a process that has already concluded; to hold otherwise would elevate procedural formalism over statutory purpose and create an absurd result Congress never intended when it enacted the 1986 exhaustion provision. Honig's recognition of futility as an exhaustion exception further supports this conclusion, and a pragmatic reading of the statutory scheme confirms that settlement-resolved IDEA claims should not operate as a perpetual bar to ADA relief.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The plain text of Section 1415(l) conditions the exhaustion requirement on a civil action 'seeking relief that is also available under this subchapter' — and where an IDEA claim has already been resolved through settlement, the administrative process has run its course, rendering further exhaustion both futile and textually inapplicable. As a textualist, I must read the statute as written: it requires exhaustion before filing, not re-exhaustion of a process already completed, and money damages — the relief Perez seeks under the ADA — are not 'available under' IDEA's subchapter, which limits remedies to prospective educational relief. Fry v. Napoleon Community Schools reinforces this reading by establishing that the gravamen inquiry asks what relief the lawsuit actually seeks, not what relief could theoretically have been sought, and Perez's ADA claim for compensatory damages falls outside IDEA's remedial scope entirely. Congress's deliberate rejection of the NSBA's broader exhaustion proposal further confirms that Section 1415(l) was not meant to sweep in claims seeking relief unavailable under IDEA, and requiring exhaustion of a completed administrative process would be an absurd result no faithful reading of the statutory text can support.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Under the gravamen test established in Fry v. Napoleon Community Schools, the IDEA exhaustion requirement under § 1415(l) applies only when the substance of a plaintiff's complaint seeks relief available under IDEA itself. Here, Perez's ADA claims seek compensatory damages — relief that IDEA hearing officers cannot provide — meaning the gravamen of his complaint falls outside IDEA's administrative framework entirely. Furthermore, requiring exhaustion after a full settlement of the underlying IDEA claim would be textually unjustifiable and practically futile, as the administrative process has already run its course and cannot provide the relief sought; Congress enacted § 1415(l) against a backdrop of well-recognized futility exceptions to statutory exhaustion requirements, and there is no sound basis in text, history, or tradition to demand a second round of administrative proceedings that can yield nothing. Institutionally, reading § 1415(l) to bar access to federal courts under these circumstances would undermine the complementary statutory scheme Congress designed when it enacted both IDEA and the ADA, frustrating rather than serving the legislative purpose of protecting disabled students' rights.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Applying the textual command of § 1415(l) alongside the 'gravamen' framework established in Fry v. Napoleon Community Schools, Perez's ADA claims seeking compensatory damages — relief categorically unavailable under IDEA — do not seek relief that IDEA can provide, and therefore the exhaustion requirement is not triggered by the statute's plain text. Section 1415(l) conditions exhaustion on whether the plaintiff seeks 'relief also available under' IDEA; because money damages are not available under IDEA, the statutory predicate for exhaustion is simply not met. Furthermore, even if one were to apply Fry's two hypothetical questions, a claim of systematic educational deprivation causing lasting harm could be pressed by an adult visitor or at a non-school public facility under the ADA, suggesting the gravamen is discrimination rather than FAPE denial. Finally, requiring exhaustion through an administrative process that has already been resolved by settlement would be a textbook case of futility recognized in Honig v. Doe, rendering any further exhaustion requirement both practically and legally inadequate.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Under Fry v. Napoleon Community Schools, the exhaustion requirement of § 1415(l) turns on whether the gravamen of the complaint seeks relief for denial of a FAPE — but critically, where an IDEA claim has already been resolved through settlement, requiring further administrative exhaustion would be both futile and contrary to the practical purposes Congress intended. Perez's ADA claims seeking compensatory damages fall outside the relief IDEA administrative proceedings can provide, and the legislative history of § 1415(l) itself confirms that exhaustion is not required when a non-IDEA claim seeks remedies unavailable in IDEA proceedings. From a procedural fairness standpoint, forcing a plaintiff who has already navigated the IDEA administrative process to exhaustion through settlement to restart that process before pursuing ADA claims would impose a meaningless procedural burden that serves none of the efficiency or expertise rationales underlying the exhaustion doctrine. My background as a public defender reinforces my concern that erecting such barriers would effectively deny disabled students meaningful access to civil rights remedies, particularly compensatory damages that address harms the IDEA framework was never designed to remedy.
